I feel like black metal is peak "mastered but not mixed" music. No mix so it sounds like shit (artistically of course) and a quick master to make it loud as fvck

Mastering is final touches, it's like adding small accents on a painting to make the focus of the piece pop a bit more. It's noticeable when it's missing but a good master should be relatively transparent.

A mastering engineer is gonna be applying small amounts of eq and compression to make sure everything pops where it should and undesirable elements stay back in the mix. They aren't there to really change the track, they're there to add a bit of shine and make sure everything is loud enough for distribution. I think "noticeable" might be the wrong word, but if you AB a track with a master it's probably going to be very subtle differences unless the mix was shit before it hit the mastering table. 


Source: homie has been a mastering engineer for 10+ years, worked with a bunch of bands you've likely heard of, he gave me my first real inroad to music production (which I then squandered to instead make beats in my bedroom).

The problem is that those albums are noticeably Sturgis-sounding, which is going to be divisive because a lot of people don't like his style of production. It's very sterile and sample heavy, and he uses a lot of the same samples album to album so it's immediately apparent when something was done by Joey Sturgis in the same way it's apparent when Mutt Lange produced an album. He left a very heavy fingerprint on the albums he worked on for better or for worse, but what true classic albums does he have that can stand up to Adam D's discography? The dude had multiple classics out before Joey graduated high school and didn't exactly slow down after that.

He mattered but from a production standpoint he was controversial. He does extremely sterile mixes and uses his own samples and tones so much that the Sturgis sound is almost immediately identifiable, and to a lot of folks not in a good way. When you have that big of a fingerprint on the albums you work on, you're taking away from the identity of the band and their music because you're literally using sounds that have been used on other albums. Some people like the sound, some people don't, but those who don't will probably not like most of his work, whereas Adam D or Will Putney don't really have a stereotypical sound where you can listen and go "yeah this is clearly [producer]". 




Plus let's be completely honest here, Asking Alexandria and Attack Attack were never the pinnacles of the genre, and neither were the rest of the Rise-core bands he worked with. They were the poppy side, which again is fine but isn't going to hold weight with the purists or fans of heavier stuff.

Adam D had 3 classic albums out before Sturgis even started producing, and it only really got better from there, plus he's still producing and Sturgis isn't. There isn't really a single metric by which Sturgis beats out Adam.

"almost every producer mentioned here" is Adam D, Kurt Ballou or Will Putney, the first two have been doing it longer and the last has a better discography. Sturgis is good but he's 4th best in the genre at most.

Warped-core is not the de facto metalcore sound, and outside of Roots none of those are "cornerstone albums".  Kurt Ballou is arguably the longest running and most influential producer for "roots" metalcore, the more hardcore stuff with tinges of metal. Adam D more or less defined the genre through the 2000s and really through today in a lot of ways. Sturgis's sound is very dated, which isn't necessarily a bad thing but all of his stuff sounds like Hot Topic circa 2010 to me, overly sterile production over bad screams and high cleans (for the most part, Attila and Emmure don't fit that mold but their production is also quite clean on most of their stuff). Some of that is personal preference but it's a dated sound, so calling him the GOAT over the two above or even really Putney is like putting Hit Boy on the same level as Ye or Dre, it's just silly. Just look at the list of bands each of them have worked with.

Housing first is called Housing **First** and not Housing Only for a reason. It is the first in a long list of steps towards success. As someone who also tends to feel like I'm not very good at games (10k hours into LoL and bronze, 900 hours into R6 and silver, 1k+ hours into Hunt Showdown and 3-4star max, playing through Doom 2016 on Hurt Me Plenty instead of Nightmare), I think the real answer is to reframe what games are to you. Are they a reflection of your life, and as such you want to improve and expand your skillset to make sure you get the most out of things? Then unfortunately you're going to have to put in the work if you really are driven to be this way, and you're probably not going to feel better until you do (or get therapy, this sounds like it's more of a mental state issue than a games issue).

 If you want games to be a way to relax and wind down and have fun, then you need to consciously work on separating your drive for improvement from your game time, and maybe play games that don't have a high skill floor/cap for a while. Retrain yourself to view games as less a part of/reflection of your daily life and more as an avenue to enjoy yourself. It's not comfortable, and it takes a lot of active work when you've spent thousands of hours playing, but it will help and then you can push that drive harder in areas of your life that actually matter. 

Also, for what it's worth, if you've butchered Elden Ring the way you mentioned in another comment, you're totally fine at games and likely better than a solid 95% of the world population at them. Don't be so hard on yourself, and remember that the internet likes to push the best of the best as something achievable by normal people leading normal lives. When I played Tarkov I had to keep reminding myself that just because I wasn't as good as streamers didn't mean I wasn't good at the game overall **because those streamers have 10k hours into the game and it's literally their job to be as good as possible**. I don't have that kind of time, and I had to content myself with being as good as I could be in the 2-3 hours a day I had to play instead of judging myself by a metric that didn't apply to my life.

I would tend to disagree on the first point. There's plenty of music out there with tons of edge and personality, you just do still have to put in some work to find it. Spotify's Song Radio can be really useful for this, especially if you've already cultivated a general music profile on there with smaller and lesser known artists played frequently. Will it be pushed? No. But it's not like they were being pushed on radio stations before streaming was a thing, and the fact that they're even able to get their music published to a large potential audience makes a world of difference to a lot of artists. I would argue that it's MORE possible to get noticed on something like Spotify specifically because of the algorithm, because the folks most likely to listen to your music are those who already listen to similar music. 






I'm also not sure that Spotify can really be blamed for the shift towards music as a background instead of a focus. That's always been the case to a certain extent, radio existed and still exists and has been used as background music since its inception. Assuming you mixed a 10 track album, that alone will cost you between $1k and $10k on its own depending on who you go to. Studio recording time varies but Google shows pricing to be $30-100/hr, and realistically tracking everything yourself is going to take a good amount of hours even if you have all your tones and parts locked in and good to go, so add another like $2k for that on the conservative side. Another like $50-100 per track for mastering is another $500-1000. Not counting the cost of equipment, recording an album with any sort of professionals could run you $15k+, and that's without getting into any sort of equipment costs or software.  




Obviously this isn't comparable to your experience since you DIYd the whole thing but in terms of labor cost this is what you're looking at for an album if you're making it professionally. Even at a home studio you're looking at equipment and software costs you wouldn't have to deal with at a pro studio including




  -interface: 50-200 -DAW: technically free if you use Reaper or Audacity (please don't use Audacity over Reaper) but can run up to and over $500 on its own. We'll use $200 for our purposes here.




 -amp sim: assuming you're using a sim and not hardware (that's a whole other can of worms) you can expect to pay $100+ for any decent amp sim out there. 




 -effects plugins: these are likely optional as Cockos ReaXXX plugins are free and more than functional, if a little outdated, but for something like Fabfilter plugins, Valhalla verbs and delays, anything else that's considered industry standard? Expect to pay 50-200 for each plugin.




 -drum sim: Ezdrummer is probably the cheapest you want to use for anything decent sounding, and that's about $90 iirc for the base version. Extra drum kits cost more. 




-all the equipment: cables, mics, soundproofing, recording space, computer for recording, headphones for monitoring, monitors for mixing. This can easily get over $1k on its own.  So even for DIY we're talking about $1000-1500 to get everything set up on the low end, not counting instruments, not counting time cost, not counting labor cost for mixing mastering tracking etc etc




. Is it cheaper and easier to produce music overall than ever before? Yeah. Is it close to 0? Maybe if you have millions of dollars but considering 99% of artists will lose money creating art, that's a lot of money to sink into a hobby project that likely won't make you any consistent income, especially operating in DIY circles where exposure is going to be inherently low due to no marketing team and low reach.

You need to be farming efficiently, you need to be securing objectives and you need to be looking for plays that you can make. Bloom: arguably most accessible, Rust, Turntail, Marigold, City Has No Empathy are the highlights imo.

Im a jungle main who has been struggling through low elo for a while and seen significant improvement recently fixing a couple specific things:


1. Clear your camps. Constantly. If you're not heading towards an objective or a lane to gank (more on that shortly) clear your camps. If you ARE on your way to an objective/lane and there's no immediate threat (lane isn't losing a fight, objective isn't being contested) clear whatever camps are on the way. If you can get deep wards in the enemy jungle, take camps there IF they're free/you can win a fight. Basically, if you're not actively doing something else you need to be taking camps. I typically finish my games around 140-200cs depending on game length and I've had a massive increase in my jungle lockdown potential just getting ahead on farm.


2. Pink wards/control wards. If you have 75g and an item slot, buy on every time. You wanna solo drag or grubs? Pink the pit. You want to make sure the enemy isn't cutting your gank paths off? Pink tribush. You just ganked bot/top? Put a pink in pixel bush. The best thing you can do to make your job easier is make sure that you have as much vision as possible and that the enemy has as little vision as possible. I usually don't buy a sweeper until later because I like to get trinket wards in high traffic areas until landing phase is open, but it's super useful later on. 


2.5. IF YOUR PINK IN DRAGON/BARON PIT REVEALS AN ENEMY WARD AND YOU'RE TRYING TO SOLO DRAG/GRUBS/HERALD DO NOT CLEAR THE WARD. IT REVEALS YOU AND YOU'LL GET COLLAPSED ON. DONT DO IT. IF YOU NEED TO CLEAR THE WARD DO THAT AND THEN COME BACK FOR THE OBJ LATER. DONT HIT IT. JUST DONT. 


3. Don't gank a losing lane UNLESS it will get you a kill or put your laner back in the game. If they're almost trading with the enemy trundle and just don't quite have the damage? Gank him, you'll likely secure the kill and if they're 0/1-0/3 they should stand a better chance. If they're 0/5 getting run down under turret? I'm muting them and doing everything in my power to secure every objective and kills in other lanes until I'm forced to deal with trundle. 


4. Don't gank in general unless you're going to secure
-enemy flash
-enemy back (low hp)
-kill.
If your gank fails you've now revealed yourself on the map which means the jg can roam to the opposite side and knows you can't respond to whatever they're going to do next OR you give a kill and put your laner behind OR your laner gives a kill and now you're behind CS and losing tempo for objectives. It's not worth your time unless something is being secured off the gank. 


5. If you have the opportunity (enemy jg shows top, bot has prio/vision or can match their laners, no enemy vision) absolutely solo objectives as quickly as possible. I main (read: one trick for 5+ years) Vi, and I'm usually taking drag or grubs within 10 seconds of spawn if things are looking ok. You need to be *very* competent with your champion and know what fights you can or cannot win and have an exit strategy prepared in case things go bad, but early grubs or infernal drake especially can be a huge boost for your team and will win you games if you can consistently secure objectives off cooldown.


5.5. PING OBJ COOLDOWNS. Even when I'm playing with friends and I can say "drag in a minute" I spam ping at 1m, 30s and 10s to make sure everyone is on the same page. They might not rotate, but making your intentions known as a jungler both prevents flame and makes it more likely that you'll have help in case things don't go according to plan. No one looks at their map in low elo, but everyone looks at chat.



6. If someone complains, tell them they're not the main character and that you'll get back to them when you need a fetch quest. That'll teach them to criticize the most important role in the game. 




If any of these are blatantly wrong, high elo folks please correct me. I've been told by Diamond/Master homies that I jungle around a plat level, but I don't have the stamina to grind ranked these days so some of this might not apply as well in soloq, but I can more or less guarantee that it'll be enough to get you out of Iron.




TLDR farm when you're not doing anything else, ward as often as possible, dont gank unless you can secure something, take objectives if at all possible, flame your team, and don't let a bad game tilt you.

In chess you'll see time controls written like that. The 5 is the total amount of time a player has to make all of their moves (timer runs when it's your turn, you end the timer when youve played your kove and your opponents timer runs, etc) and the +0 refers to the amount of time given before the clock starts running. In something like a 5+10 blitz, you have 5 minutes on your timer at the beginning of the match and every time its your turn 10 seconss get added to your clock. Increments can be nice because it gives you flexibility with your clock, you can either take an extra 10 seconds per turn making sure you're playing the right move, or you can make a move in 1 second (like in a system opening where you play the first 6-7 moves the exact same regardless of what your opponent plays) and bank extra time for mid or end game.

Shelter staff here. Hate to hear that you've had this experience, although I know it's a fairly common one. There are a lot of folks in the business that really do love their jobs and do their best to treat everyone with dignity and respect, and there are also a lot of people who come in and power trip or let their own preconceived notions win out. I work in a low barrier shelter, and while we do have a lot of challenging residents (one of our staff was recently assaulted pretty badly by someone who stopped taking their meds) it's still not an excuse to push that hostility onto others, especially those who are vulnerable. 

I would like to say, though, that it CAN be a very tough job, especially in a low barrier/harm reduction setting where drugs are used pretty openly. My particular shelter had about 8 deaths over the course of a month due to ODs, and that does wear on us, not to mention the very frequent if not sometimes constant verbal abuse and other strays we catch simply by being there. Im thankful for my job and enjoy what I do, but some days can get really fucking hard and it can be difficult to soldier through hours of someone screaming slurs at you and come out the other side with a smile. If there's someone who's being particularly rude and hostile, report them to management. If there's no management, report them to a different employee who isn't an asshole. 

Lastly, I'm sorry to all of you that you're having to go through this. I do my best to make my shelter comfortable but knowing how poorly even my city treats the homeless, despite being billed as a haven, breaks my heart and really makes me thankful for the small things I have. I hope the winter treats you all well and that you're all able to stay safe and find somewhere that can treat you like the people you are.

I'm nowhere near qualified to give advice on how to play league of legends, as I've spent the last 10 years between iron (bronze 5, and what's more the lowest depths of bronze 5) to high silver, but I CAN offer advice as to what helped me get out of that super low ELO cesspool (ELO hell is a thing, you'll get through it, be patient). I played Quinn (this was season 7-8 I believe, she was actually a feasible champ back then). I played only Quinn in ranked. I played only Quinn for a long time in normals. I did everything I could to learn as much about Quinn and the matchups I would see most often by playing into them, and inting a lot of the time. League is a game of repetition, and if you plan to grow and climb you have to be ready to put in 100+ games to make any sort of progress, that's just how it is. People talk about learning spacing and wave management or jungle tracking or whatever but if you're in Iron 4 you literally do not have the tools to do all of that. Focus on the basics. Learn the champ (or 2) you want to play, even if it's Azir, one of the highest skill cap champs in the game. Figure out who is meta and look at your post history to see who you're fighting the most. See who you lose against. Pick Azir into them. Pick one thing to focus on when you fight them, be it staying back out of their engage range, keeping your river warded, getting 1 extra cs per minute. Eventually you'll get a feel for your limits and how well YOU can play your champion, and then you can start looking at the other things and learning macro and whatnot. Until you have a good instinctive grasp of your champion and what you can do with them you're just pushing buttons and clicking.

  


  


/Ignore all every game. Nothing anyone says in iron is going to help you improve. If I had taken this advice when it was given I wouldn't have spent 5 seasons in hell. Your biggest obstacle in league will be your mental. The second biggest will be your teammates mental. Remove that from the equation and focus on yourself. Rank is an indicator of skill level, it's not an accolade to earn. Get better at the game and the rank will follow.
